blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A CSV exporter, for every cell, calls `row.getClass().getMethod(getterName)`, then `setAccessible(true)`, then `invoke(row)`. It writes 3 million cells a minute from a few dozen row classes. Which single change removes most of the reflective cost per cell?

options.text: Keeping each `Method` in a map after its first lookup, since the lookup searches the class and builds a new `Method` on every call
options.says: the lookup cost about 22 ns and 168 bytes per call, four times the call itself; getMethod returns a new copy each time

options.text: Keeping each `Method` in a map after its first lookup, since a `Method` read from the map for every cell is a constant the JIT inlines through
options.says: a Method read from a map or a non-final field is not a constant to the JIT; only a static final field or a record component reached through one is

options.text: Calling `setAccessible(true)` once per `Method` instead of per cell, since each call repeats the module access checks
options.says: repeating setAccessible before every call cost at most half a nanosecond, within the spread between JVMs, against about 22 ns for the lookup

options.text: Calling `setAccessible(true)` once per `Method` instead of per cell, since each call for every cell stops the JIT from compiling `invoke`
options.says: setAccessible only sets the copy's flag; repeating it cost at most half a nanosecond, and the expensive part is the lookup

origin.section: Looking a Method Up Costs More Than Calling It, So Look Up Once

questions.stem: On JDK 21, a warmed loop calls `holder.getter.invoke(dto)` 10 million times, where `holder` is an instance of an ordinary class with a field `final Method getter`. A colleague changes the loop to `GETTER.invoke(dto)`, where `GETTER` is a `private static final Method` of the loop's class. What should the next run show?

options.text: About the same time per call, since a static final field and a final instance field are both constants to the JIT
options.says: HotSpot doesn't trust an ordinary final instance field, which reflection can write; a Method there costs as much as one in a non-final field

options.text: About the same time per call, since from JDK 18 every `invoke` goes through a method handle whatever holds the `Method`
options.says: invoke does go through a method handle, but the JIT inlines through it only when the Method is a constant

options.text: Several times less per call, since the JIT trusts a static final field and inlines the target through the `Method`
options.says: invokeConstant 1.1 to 1.4 ns against invokeClassFinal 4.6 to 5 ns

options.text: Several times less per call, since a `Method` in a static final field skips the access check made through an instance field
options.says: where a Method is kept doesn't change the access check; setAccessible(true) skips it, and that saved only fractions of a nanosecond

origin.section: Since JDK 18, Method.invoke Is Fast Only When the JIT Sees a Constant

questions.stem: A load test of a reflective mapper passes entity ids 0 to 99 to `Method.invoke` on methods that take and return `int`, and its allocation profile shows nothing from `invoke`. In production the ids have seven digits. What does the production profile show for those calls?

options.text: Allocation from `invoke`, since each id and each result outside -128 to 127 becomes a new `Integer`
options.says: each value outside the Integer cache costs a 16-byte Integer; small values come from the cache

options.text: Allocation from `invoke`, since escape analysis keeps the argument array once a value falls outside -128 to 127
options.says: escape analysis removed the Object[] for small and large values alike; it was 24 bytes only with escape analysis turned off

options.text: Nothing from `invoke`, since escape analysis removes the boxes for values outside -128 to 127 as well as inside
options.says: escape analysis removed the array, but the Integers for values outside the cache stayed: 32 bytes per call

options.text: Nothing from `invoke`, since from JDK 18 `invoke` hands ids of any size to the method handle without boxing them
options.says: invoke takes Object... and returns Object, so primitives are boxed; only invokeExact on a handle passes them as they are

origin.section: A Method Handle Obeys the Same Rule, and invokeExact Never Boxes

questions.stem: After a move from JDK 17 to JDK 21, a micro-benchmark of a command dispatcher, which calls one handler `Method` kept in a field, got 2.5 times slower, and `-Djdk.reflect.useDirectMethodHandle=false` brings the old time back. In production the dispatcher sends every command's handler method through that same `invoke` call site. What should the team expect from the flag in production?

options.text: The same gain, since the flag gives each of several handlers at that call site a generated accessor the JIT inlines
options.says: the generated accessor was inlined only while one Method used the call site; with several it was not

options.text: The same gain, since the flag makes the JIT treat several handler `Method`s at that call site as constants, as it did the one
options.says: the flag changes the implementation behind invoke, not what the JIT treats as a constant

options.text: Little or no gain, since with several handlers at that call site the old generated accessors are not inlined either
options.says: with three other Methods through the loop first, the old implementation was about as fast as the new one and allocated 56 bytes a call

options.text: Little or no gain, since with several handlers at that call site the flag only changes how each one's first calls are made
options.says: the flag replaces the whole implementation: native calls first, then a generated accessor class per Method

origin.section: The Pre-JDK 18 Reflection Won Only While One Method Used the Call Site

questions.stem: A teammate times a direct call and `invoke` on a `static final Method`, each as `for (int i = 0; i < 50_000_000; i++) { int r = call(i); }` after warm-up rounds. Both report 0.00 ns per call. What does the comparison establish?

options.text: That both cost the same, since the JIT inlines a call through a static final `Method` as it does a direct call
options.says: with results used, a constant Method cost about five times a direct call; the zero says the loops were removed

options.text: That both cost the same, since storing every result in `r` keeps the JIT from removing either call
options.says: a result stored in a local nobody reads is not used; the JIT deleted the direct loop that threw its result away

options.text: Nothing about either cost, since a result stored in `r` and never read lets the JIT drop the work
options.says: the direct loop with its result thrown away measured 0.00 ns: the JIT deleted it

options.text: Nothing about either cost, since 50 million calls take too little time for `System.nanoTime` to resolve
options.says: the harness reports nanoseconds per call over rounds of 20 million calls, and the direct loop that used its results measured 0.21 ns

origin.section: A Loop Whose Result Nobody Reads Measures Nothing

concepts: Since JDK 18 Method.invoke calls through a method handle, and the JIT inlines it only when the Method is a constant: a static final field or a record component reached through one, not a final field of an ordinary class.

On JDK 21 -Djdk.reflect.useDirectMethodHandle=false brings back the pre-JDK 18 implementation, which beats the new one only while a single Method passes through the call site; JDK 25 ignores the flag.

setAccessible(true) skips the access check inside invoke and saves under a nanosecond; repeating it before every call costs nothing measurable, so the lookup, not the flag, is what to cache for speed.
A timed loop whose results are never used can be deleted by the JIT and measures nothing; a harness warms up, uses every result and compares in fresh JVMs.
